prompt: A table has a column `email` that is unique and never null, and a column `id` that is the primary key. What is `email` called?
hint: The word is about the possibility, not about which one was chosen.

choices.text: A candidate key
choices.why: Any column set that could have been the primary key is a candidate key; one of them was chosen.

choices.text: A foreign key
choices.why: A foreign key points at another table's key. Nothing here points anywhere.

choices.text: A surrogate key
choices.why: That is `id`: a value with no meaning outside the database, invented to be the key.

choices.text: A partial key
choices.why: There is no such thing in the relational model.

prompt: Why does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to unknown rather than to true?
hint: Think about what the value is standing in for.

choices.text: Because the comparison is deferred to the index
choices.why: Nothing about this involves an index.

choices.text: A null is an absence, not a value
choices.why: Two unknown ages are not an assertion that the ages match, so the comparison has nothing to stand on.

choices.text: Because the standard reserves the case
choices.why: It falls out of three-valued logic rather than being a special case.

choices.text: Because SQL compares nulls by identity
choices.why: There is no identity to compare; there is no value.

prompt: An `orders.customer_id` foreign key is declared `ON DELETE RESTRICT`. A customer with three orders is deleted. What happens?
hint: Two of these describe a different clause.

choices.text: The orders are deleted with the customer
choices.why: That is CASCADE.

choices.text: The `customer_id` on the three orders becomes null
choices.why: That is SET NULL.

choices.text: The orders are kept and point at a customer that is gone
choices.why: That is precisely the state a foreign key exists to prevent.

choices.text: The delete is refused
choices.why: RESTRICT refuses while a child row still points at the parent.

prompt: Match each constraint to what it refuses.
hint: One of them is about a row's relationship with another table.

pairs.right: A reference to a row that is not there
A value outside a rule you wrote
A second row with the same value

right_distractors: A write while another transaction reads
A column added to a full table

prompt: A junction table records which students are enrolled on which courses, one row per enrolment. What should its primary key be?
hint: What makes one row of this table different from another?

choices.text: `student_id` alone
choices.why: A student takes more than one course.

choices.text: An added `id` column
choices.why: It permits the same pair twice, which is the one thing this table must not allow.

choices.text: The pair `(student_id, course_id)`
choices.why: The pair is what a row asserts, so the pair is the identity.

choices.text: `course_id` alone
choices.why: A course has more than one student.

prompt: In the relational model the formal word for a table is a ___, and the formal word for one of its rows is a ___.
hint: One names the set; the other names a member of it.

prompt: You are told a natural key — the citizen's tax number — is better than a surrogate `id` because it carries meaning. What is the strongest argument against it?
hint: Think about what happens after the row is written.

choices.text: It is refused as a unique constraint
choices.why: It is accepted as one.

choices.text: The correction has to reach every row that points at it
choices.why: A tax number entered wrongly is corrected sometimes, and a key that carries meaning inherits every correction that meaning needs.

choices.text: It is slower to index, and the index can be large
choices.why: Marginal, and not the reason.

choices.text: It is longer to type, so it tends to be mistyped
choices.why: True and trivial.

prompt: What does it mean to say a relational table has no inherent order?
hint: What has to be written for an order to exist?

choices.text: An ORDER BY is applied to every query automatically
choices.why: It is not.

choices.text: Rows come back in the order they were inserted, unless a page was reused
choices.why: That is common and never promised, which is worse than it being false.

choices.text: Without ORDER BY, no order is promised
choices.why: Any order you observe is an accident of the plan and may change with the data or the version.

choices.text: Rows are stored alphabetically until an index says otherwise
choices.why: Nothing stores them alphabetically.

prompt: A table of orders stores `customer_id`, `customer_name` and `customer_city`. Which normal form does this break, and why?
hint: The customer's name depends on which customer, not on which order.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: The repetition here is exactly what third normal form is about.

choices.text: Second, because part of a composite key determines a column
choices.why: That needs a composite key, and this table has a single-column one.

choices.text: First, because a column holds more than one value
choices.why: Each of these holds one value.

choices.text: Third: a non-key column determines another
choices.why: `customer_id` determines the name and the city, and it is not the key of this table.

prompt: A `phones` column holds the string `'11 9999-0000, 11 8888-1111'`. Which normal form is broken?
hint: Count the values in one cell.

choices.text: The first
choices.why: A cell holds one value, and this holds two.

choices.text: The second
choices.why: That is about partial dependency on a composite key.

choices.text: The third
choices.why: That is about a non-key column determining another.

choices.text: Boyce-Codd
choices.why: That is a stricter version of the third, about overlapping candidate keys.

prompt: An invoice line stores the product's price at the time of sale, and the product table also has a price. A reviewer calls this a third normal form violation. Are they right?
hint: Ask whether the two numbers are the same fact.

choices.text: No — the third normal form applies to keys rather than to values
choices.why: It applies to every non-key column.

choices.text: Yes — any repeated column breaks the third normal form
choices.why: Normal forms are about dependency, not about a column name appearing twice.

choices.text: Yes — the price is derivable from the product
choices.why: Today's price is. The price on a sale from last March is not.

choices.text: No — the two are different facts
choices.why: The price on the line is what was charged; the price on the product is what it costs today. One is history and cannot be recomputed from the other.

prompt: What does a deliberate denormalisation cost that a normalised design does not?
hint: Think about what happens on a write.

choices.text: More disk, and the backup time that comes with it
choices.why: Disk is the cheap half.

choices.text: Every write has to update the copy too
choices.why: A missed one is a lie nothing reports: the duplicate is yours to keep true, on every path that writes, forever.

choices.text: A slower read on the duplicated column
choices.why: The read is what it buys, not what it costs.

choices.text: The loss of foreign keys on the table
choices.why: Nothing about a copy removes a constraint.

prompt: Put these four states of one table in order, from least normalised to most.
items: A `tags` column holding a comma-separated list
One row per tag, with the article's title repeated on each
One row per tag, with the article's id and its title
A `tags` table and a junction table, with no title copied
trap: The middle two look interchangeable: both have one row per tag, and the difference is whether what is repeated is the key or the words.

prompt: A reporting query joins seven tables and takes four seconds. Which is the honest first question before denormalising?
hint: One of these is free to answer and the rest are work.

choices.text: Whether the indexes the plan wants are there
choices.why: Most seven-table joins are slow because one of them is a sequential scan, and reading the plan says which.

choices.text: Whether to move to a wider machine
choices.why: Hardware buys a constant factor and hides the reason.

choices.text: Whether to add a summary table
choices.why: That is a decision to take after you know why it is slow.

choices.text: Whether to cache the result for five minutes
choices.why: That makes the report stale rather than fast.

prompt: Why should money be stored as `numeric` rather than as `float`?
hint: Ask what the type promises about arithmetic.

choices.text: A float is limited to six digits
choices.why: A double carries about fifteen.

choices.text: A float is refused in a CHECK constraint on a money column
choices.why: It is accepted.

choices.text: A float has no exact 0.10, so sums drift
choices.why: Binary floating point cannot represent a tenth, and the error accumulates across a ledger until a total is visibly wrong.

choices.text: A float is slower to add
choices.why: It is faster, which is the temptation.

prompt: A column is `timestamp without time zone` and the application writes local times from two countries. What has been lost?
hint: Two readings of one number.

choices.text: The ability to sort the column
choices.why: It sorts. It sorts wrongly, which is the problem.

choices.text: The ability to index the column
choices.why: It indexes.

choices.text: Which instant each row is about
choices.why: Without the offset, 09:00 in São Paulo and 09:00 in Lisbon are the same stored number and different moments.

choices.text: The precision below the second
choices.why: Precision is a separate property and is still there.

prompt: Match each ALTER TABLE to the work it does on a large table.
hint: One only writes a line in the catalogue.

pairs.left: ADD COLUMN with a volatile default

pairs.right: Reads every row and writes none
Marks it dead and reclaims the space later

right_distractors: Runs without any lock at all
Is refused while the table has rows

prompt: A constraint added as NOT VALID skips the check on the rows that are already there. To check them afterwards without blocking writes you run ALTER TABLE … ___ CONSTRAINT.
hint: One word, and it is not `CHECK`.

prompt: What is the difference between `varchar(50)` and `text` in PostgreSQL?
hint: One of them refuses something.

choices.text: The length limit, and nothing in how it is stored
choices.why: They share a storage format; the limit is a constraint expressed in the type.

choices.text: `varchar` is stored inline and `text` out of line
choices.why: Both follow the same rule, decided by size rather than by type.

choices.text: `text` cannot be indexed
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: `varchar` is faster for short strings
choices.why: It is not measurably faster.

prompt: A CHECK constraint and application-level validation both express one rule. Why keep the CHECK?
hint: Count the ways a row can arrive.

choices.text: The CHECK is faster than the application's test
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: Other writers reach the table too
choices.why: A migration, a script and a second service each write here, and the constraint is the only rule all of them meet.

choices.text: The CHECK lets the planner skip rows it knows cannot match
choices.why: A CHECK can inform the planner, and that is a side effect rather than the reason.

choices.text: The CHECK gives a better error message
choices.why: It usually gives a worse one.

prompt: `WHERE status <> 'shipped'` returns fewer rows than expected. What is the most likely reason?
hint: Something in the column is neither equal nor unequal.

choices.text: A trailing space in the literal
choices.why: Possible, and it would not single out a whole group of rows.

choices.text: A case difference in the stored values
choices.why: That would be a reason, and it would change which rows match rather than silently dropping a class of them.

choices.text: A missing index on `status`
choices.why: An index changes speed and never the result.

choices.text: Rows where `status` is null
choices.why: A null compares to nothing, so `<>` is unknown and the row is dropped.

prompt: A page of results uses `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`. Two rows share the same `created_at`. What can go wrong?
hint: What decides the order between the two of them?

choices.text: The rows come back in insertion order
choices.why: Nothing promises that.

choices.text: The query is refused as ambiguous by the planner
choices.why: It runs.

choices.text: A row appears twice, or not at all
choices.why: The tie is broken by the plan, which may differ between the two queries that fetch the two pages.

choices.text: The second page is always empty
choices.why: It is not.

prompt: Which of these WHERE clauses lets an index on `created_at` be used?
hint: One side of the comparison has to be the bare column.

choices.text: `WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-02'`
choices.why: The column stands alone, so the index range applies.

choices.text: `WHERE created_at + interval '1 day' > now()`
choices.why: The arithmetic is on the column rather than on the constant.

choices.text: `WHERE extract(year from created_at) = 2026`
choices.why: Same problem: the column is inside a function.

choices.text: `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-03-01'`
choices.why: The function wraps the column, so the index on the raw value no longer matches.

prompt: To bring back rows whose `name` starts with the letters `an` and ignores what follows, you write WHERE name LIKE ___ — and the wildcard for a single character is ___.
hint: Two symbols, and one of them is a single character.

prompt: What does `SELECT DISTINCT a, b` do?
hint: Read it as one thing rather than two.

choices.text: Removes repeats in each column separately
choices.why: That would produce columns of different lengths, which is not a table.

choices.text: Removes repeated pairs of `a` and `b`
choices.why: DISTINCT applies to the whole row the select produces, not to one column.

choices.text: Sorts the result and removes neighbouring repeats
choices.why: A sort is one way to implement it and is not promised.

choices.text: Removes repeated values of `a` only
choices.why: That would need a different construct.

prompt: `ORDER BY name` puts `Ana` before `ana` on one server and after it on another. What explains it?
hint: Something about the database decides what order letters are in.

choices.text: The version of the SQL standard each one follows
choices.why: The standard leaves this to the collation.

choices.text: The client's locale
choices.why: The sort happens on the server.

choices.text: Whether an index exists on `name`
choices.why: An index follows the collation rather than deciding it.

choices.text: The collation it was created with
choices.why: Ordering text is a property of the collation, and two servers can be set up with different ones.

prompt: A LEFT JOIN is written with the filter on the right table in the WHERE clause instead of in the ON clause. What does that do?
hint: Ask when each of the two is applied.

choices.text: It is refused by the parser as ambiguous
choices.why: It runs without a word of complaint.

choices.text: It leaves the result the same on both sides
choices.why: That is true of an inner join and false here.

choices.text: It turns the join into an inner join
choices.why: The unmatched rows come back with nulls and the WHERE then drops them, which is what an inner join does.

choices.text: It makes the join faster on a large table
choices.why: It changes the result, which is worse than changing the speed.

prompt: Table A has 3 rows, table B has 4, and each A row matches exactly 2 B rows. How many rows does an inner join produce?
hint: Count per row of A.

choices.why: That adds the two counts instead of multiplying the matches.
Three rows of A, two matches each.
That is the cross join, which is every pair.
That is the size of B.

prompt: A report joins `orders` to `order_items` and sums `orders.total`. The totals come out far too high. What happened?
hint: Think about how many times each order row appears.

choices.text: The order's total is counted once per item
choices.why: The join repeats the order row for every item, and the sum adds each copy.

choices.text: The join lost the rows with no items
choices.why: That would lower the total.

choices.text: Some orders have a null total
choices.why: A null would pull the sum down rather than up.

choices.text: The totals are stored in cents
choices.why: That would be a constant factor of a hundred and the same every time.

prompt: Match each join to which unmatched rows it keeps.
hint: One of them keeps none.
right_distractors: Only the ones with a null key
Only the first match of each

prompt: You want customers who have never placed an order. Which of these gets it wrong?
hint: One of them behaves differently when a null turns up in the subquery.

choices.text: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id)`
choices.why: EXISTS is about whether a row is there, so a null is simply a row that does not match.

choices.text: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)`
choices.why: The null is excluded, so NOT IN behaves.

choices.text: A LEFT JOIN with `WHERE o.id IS NULL`
choices.why: The anti-join written by hand, and it is correct.

choices.text: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`
choices.why: One null `customer_id` makes NOT IN return no rows at all, silently.

prompt: A join of a table with itself needs each side to be given a different name. The keyword for that name is ___, and the join that produces every possible pair is called a ___ join.
hint: The second one is two words in some dialects and one here.

prompt: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
hint: One of them can see the aggregate.

choices.text: HAVING is the older spelling of WHERE
choices.why: They are different clauses at different stages.

choices.text: HAVING filters rows, WHERE filters groups
choices.why: The two are the other way round.

choices.text: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
choices.why: WHERE runs before the grouping, so it cannot see a count; HAVING runs after.

choices.text: WHERE is refused when GROUP BY is present
choices.why: It is accepted, and it is usually what you want.

prompt: A column holds 10 rows, three of them null. What do `count(*)` and `count(column)` return?
hint: One of them counts rows and the other counts values.

choices.text: 7 and 10
choices.why: The two are the other way round.

choices.text: 10 and 7
choices.why: The star counts rows; the column counts the values that are there.

choices.text: 10 and 10
choices.why: That would make the two spellings the same.

choices.text: 7 and 7
choices.why: The star is not affected by a null in any column.

prompt: What does a window function do that GROUP BY does not?
hint: Count the rows that come back.

choices.text: It keeps every row and adds the aggregate beside it
choices.why: A group collapses its rows into one; a window leaves them and computes over a frame.

choices.text: It can be used inside a WHERE clause
choices.why: It cannot: the window is computed after the WHERE.

choices.text: It works without an ORDER BY
choices.why: So does a GROUP BY.

choices.text: It computes faster over a large table
choices.why: Speed is not the distinction and often goes the other way.

prompt: Match each ranking function to how it numbers a tie of two rows followed by a third.
hint: Two of them agree on the tie and disagree on what comes next.

prompt: `SELECT department, name, count(*) FROM staff GROUP BY department` is refused. Why?
hint: One column is neither grouped nor aggregated.

choices.text: A GROUP BY needs at least two columns
choices.why: One is fine.

choices.text: `department` has to be repeated in an ORDER BY
choices.why: Ordering is a separate matter.

choices.text: `count(*)` needs an alias before it can be selected
choices.why: An alias is a convenience.

choices.text: `name` is neither in the GROUP BY nor inside an aggregate
choices.why: The group has many names and the query does not say which one to show.

prompt: A table of 1000 sales has 4 regions. A query groups by region and takes the average. How many rows does it return?
hint: One per group.

prompt: What distinguishes a correlated subquery from an uncorrelated one?
hint: Ask how many times it has to be evaluated.

choices.text: It appears in the FROM clause
choices.why: That is a derived table and is a separate thing.

choices.text: It returns more than one column
choices.why: Either kind can.

choices.text: It refers to a column of the outer query
choices.why: That reference is what ties it to each outer row, so it is evaluated per row.

choices.text: It is written with the EXISTS keyword
choices.why: EXISTS is common there and is not the definition.

prompt: A view is described as 'a stored query, not stored data'. What follows from that?
hint: Ask what happens when the underlying table changes.

choices.text: Reading it runs the query again, so it is always current and never faster
choices.why: There is nothing stored to go stale and nothing stored to read quickly.

choices.text: Reading it is faster because the plan is kept
choices.why: That is closer to a materialised view, and even there the plan is not the point.

choices.text: It cannot be used inside another query
choices.why: It is used exactly like a table.

choices.text: It has to be refreshed after a write
choices.why: That is a materialised view.

prompt: A recursive CTE is written to walk a tree of categories and never finishes. What is the most likely cause?
hint: Something about the data rather than about the SQL.

choices.text: The base case selects too many rows
choices.why: A large base case finishes.

choices.text: The UNION ALL should have been UNION
choices.why: UNION would mask a cycle by removing duplicates, which is a patch rather than the cause.

choices.text: A missing index on the parent column
choices.why: That makes it slow and not endless.

choices.text: A cycle in the parent references
choices.why: A category that is its own ancestor makes the recursion produce rows for ever.

prompt: When is a materialised view the right answer rather than a plain view?
hint: Two conditions have to hold together.

choices.text: The query is expensive, whatever the freshness requirement
choices.why: Serving stale numbers to somebody who needs current ones is worse than being slow.

choices.text: The query is expensive and the data is allowed to be a little old
choices.why: Both halves are needed: the cost is what it buys back, and the staleness is what it costs.

choices.text: The data is allowed to be old, whatever the query costs
choices.why: A cheap query gains nothing and adds a refresh to maintain.

choices.text: The underlying tables are small and rarely written
choices.why: Then the plain view is already fast.
